messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marta was a 28-year-old police officer of European background who had come to treatment after months of feeling as if she were no longer fully living in her own life. The index event occurred during a late-night operation in which she and a trusted senior officer responded to what should have been a routine call. In the chaos that followed, police violence erupted suddenly and from the very people she had believed would keep order and protect her. She described the moment as shocking not only for what happened, but for how completely it shattered her sense of who could be trusted. Since then, she had come to believe that her body had not received the message that the danger was over: it kept bracing, scanning, and reacting as though she were still in the middle of that scene, even in ordinary, safe moments at home or on shift.

The memory of the incident did not return to Marta as a normal recollection. It forced its way into her mind without warning, and when it did, it arrived with a full sensory force that made it feel completely real all at once. She would be standing in the station kitchen or sitting beside her partner on the sofa and suddenly be back in the same sounds, smells, and bodily sensations from the night of the event, as though the scene had broken open around her. What unnerved her most was that the memory felt alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her; she could recount it, but it did not feel like something her own life should contain. The more she tried to push it away, the more sharply it appeared, and she began to fear the moments when her mind went quiet because that was often when it would intrude.

As the months passed, Marta’s understanding of herself and the world hardened around those experiences. She became increasingly certain that the world was a dangerous place and that safety was fragile, a temporary state that could be taken away in an instant. Her body’s constant alarm seemed to confirm that belief for her. Even when she knew she was in her own apartment or walking with her partner through a familiar neighborhood, her heart could start racing and her muscles would tighten before she had time to think. She interpreted these reactions as proof that she was still in danger, and that her own body was now an unreliable witness, always anticipating threat before she consciously registered it. That sense of bodily betrayal deepened her fear and made the intrusive memory feel even more credible, as if the memory and her physical state were proving the same terrible point together.

The memory and her appraisals became tightly bound in the way Marta moved through daily life. After the first few episodes, she started avoiding anything that might set off another flood of sensory recollection, including certain routes near the station and the particular locker room where she had been standing afterward. At work, she found herself watching colleagues more closely than before, reading for signs of tension or hostility, and her vigilance only seemed to keep the event active in her mind. When a radio burst of static sounded unexpectedly during a shift, she was jolted back into the scene so vividly that she had to grip the counter to stay oriented; afterward, she could not stop thinking that if her body could react so strongly, then the danger must still be close. On quieter evenings, if she noticed her chest tightening or her shoulders rising, she took that as further evidence that she was unsafe, and the more she made sense of her symptoms as warnings, the more power the memory seemed to have over her. Marta began to withdraw from casual social plans, not wanting her partner to see her lose control, and she worried that the part of her that had once felt capable and steady had been replaced by someone permanently on guard.

By the time she sought help, Marta was exhausted by the intensity of the intrusions and by the conviction that her own body was working against her. She had become afraid that if this kept going, she would not be able to stay effective in her job or remain present in her relationship. What finally brought her in was the worsening frequency of the memories and the growing certainty that she could not keep managing them alone. She wanted relief from the episodes that arrived without permission, and she was most afraid that the world would continue to feel unsafe no matter where she stood, leaving her trapped in a life where every bodily reaction seemed to announce another betrayal.
